etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin dictātus, perfect passive participle of dictō (“pronounce or declare repeatedly; dictate”), frequentative of dīcō (“say, speak”).

quote.citation: 2001, Sydney I. Landau, Dictionaries: The Art and Craft of Lexicography, Cambridge University Press, →ISBN, page 409:
quote.text: Trademark Owners will nevertheless try to dictate how their marks are to be represented, but dictionary publishers with spine can resist such pressure.

definitions.definition: To speak in order for someone to write down the words.

quote.citation: 1837, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], “Return to Courtenaye Hall”, in Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides. […], volume III, London: Henry Colburn, […], →OCLC, page 151:
quote.text: He had offered, and been refused! There was that in her own nature, which sympathised with the pride, for such she held to be the motive, dictating the refusal.

quote.citation: 1961 December, “The Channel Tunnel—a realistic proposal”, in Trains Illustrated, page 723:
quote.text: Geology dictates the approximate location of the tunnel.

quote.citation: 1977 August 20, David Holland, quoting Tony Bosco, “Tony Bosco”, in Gay Community News, volume 5, number 7, page 19:
quote.text: I didn't lay this bar, or the restaurant for that matter, out on paper. The design was dictated by the materials.
